summary: Defines the addressing architecture of IP version 6. It was a standards-track document, is now historic, and was replaced by RFC 2373.

eli5.summary: The rules about how addresses in the next-generation Internet are written and sorted.

questions: what is the difference between unicast anycast and multicast
subtitle: How the next-generation Internet numbers and routes its devices.

tldr.problem: IPv4 was running out of addresses because it could only create 4.3 billion unique numbers, but the Internet needed more. IPv6 was designed with vastly more address space, but needed a clear specification of how addresses would be structured and assigned.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (16 times larger than IPv4's 32 bits) to create approximately 340 undecillion unique addresses. The specification defines three address types (unicast, anycast and multicast), notation conventions, and hierarchical address allocation with prefixes for different purposes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1884 provided the first formal addressing specification for IPv6 but was quickly updated as IPv6 was refined in deployment planning.

today: RFC 1884 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 2373 in 1998 as IPv6 addressing was refined. The basic principles remain the same, but later specifications clarified and extended the allocation and usage rules.

sections.title: IPv6 Addresses and Their Types
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for individual interfaces or groups of interfaces. There are three types: Unicast addresses identify a single interface and packets are delivered to that one device. Anycast addresses identify a group of interfaces, and a packet is delivered to the nearest one according to routing distance. Multicast addresses identify a group, and packets are delivered to all interfaces in that group. Unlike IPv4, IPv6 has no broadcast type; multicast addresses serve that role.

Addresses are assigned to network interfaces, not to nodes themselves. A single node can have multiple interfaces, each with its own address. Addresses are assigned as part of the on-network link layer.
sections.eli5: An IPv6 address is a unique number for a device on the Internet. Some addresses talk to one device (unicast), some talk to the nearest device in a group (anycast), and some talk to all devices in a group (multicast).

sections.title: Writing IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are written in one of three standard forms. The preferred form is eight 16-bit groups in hexadecimal separated by colons: FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210. Leading zeros in each group can be omitted, but at least one digit must appear in every group.

The second form uses the :: notation to compress consecutive groups of zeros. For example, 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A becomes 1080::8:800:200C:417A. The :: can only appear once in an address and can compress leading or trailing zeros. Examples: ::1 for the loopback address and :: for the unspecified address.

The third form mixes IPv6 and IPv4 notation for addresses that carry IPv4 addresses inside them: x:x:x:x:x:x:d.d.d.d, where the last four decimal groups are standard IPv4 notation. Example: ::FFFF:129.144.52.38.
sections.eli5: IPv6 addresses are long numbers written in hexadecimal (using digits 0-9 and letters A-F). You can write them in three ways: the full way with all groups, a shortened way using :: for zeros, or a mixed way that includes an IPv4 address at the end.

sections.title: Unicast Addresses and Hierarchical Allocation
sections.content:
Unicast addresses are organized hierarchically by leading bit prefixes called the Format Prefix (FP). The first few bits of an address indicate its type and allocation purpose. The specification initially allocates 15% of the 128-bit address space with the remainder reserved for future use.

Major unicast address types include: Provider-Based Global Unicast Addresses (prefix 010) assigned by internet service providers for globally routable addresses; IPv6 Addresses with Embedded IPv4 Addresses (prefix 0000:0000) for transitional use alongside IPv4; Link-Local Use Addresses (prefix 1111 1110 10) for local network segments; and Site-Local Use Addresses (prefix 1111 1110 11) for organization-internal use.

Simple hosts may view their own address as having no internal structure, while more sophisticated hosts and routers understand hierarchical boundaries with subnet prefixes and interface identifiers within a subnet.
sections.eli5: IPv6 addresses are organized like postal codes: the first digits say what region (country, provider, etc.) the address is in, the middle digits narrow it down further (a city, a subnet), and the last digits are the specific device. Different types of addresses start with different patterns of leading digits.

sections.title: Anycast and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Anycast addresses are taken from the unicast address space and are not syntactically distinguished from unicast addresses. An anycast address identifies a set of interfaces (usually on different nodes), and a packet sent to that address is delivered to the nearest one as determined by routing protocols. A required anycast address is the Subnet-Router Anycast Address, which is formed from any subnet prefix by setting the remaining bits to zero. This allows any router on a subnet to receive traffic designated for that subnet.

Multicast addresses (prefix 1111 1111) identify a group of interfaces. Packets are delivered to all interfaces in the group. Pre-defined multicast addresses include well-known groups like all-nodes on a link (FF02::1), all-routers on a link (FF02::2), and solicited-node addresses used in neighbor discovery (FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF00:0/104).
sections.eli5: Anycast is like 'delivery to the nearest post office' - a package goes to whichever office is closest. Multicast is like a group broadcast - a message goes to everyone in the group. Both use special address patterns to work.

sections.title: Addresses Every Node Must Have
sections.content:
Every IPv6 node must have at least two required unicast addresses: a loopback address (::1) for communication within the node itself, and a link-local address formed from the link-local prefix and a 64-bit interface identifier. The link-local address allows the node to communicate on its local network segment even before global addresses are assigned.

Nodes are expected to have additional unicast addresses such as one or more global unicast addresses for communication across the Internet. Hosts should be aware of subnet prefixes for the links they are attached to in order to determine which destinations are on the local link versus remote.
sections.eli5: Every device on IPv6 must have at least a loopback address (for talking to itself) and a link-local address (for talking to neighbors on the same network link), even if it doesn't have an address for the whole Internet yet.
